others.route: Atypical Working Scheme permission (beyond 90 days, an Employment Permit)

note: Ireland: EEA and Swiss nationals live and work freely (the eea list), and British citizens under the Common Travel Area. A non-EEA performer needs a permission: for short-term work (generally under 90 days, the entertainment industry included) the Department of Justice's Atypical Working Scheme, for at most 90 days over six months; for longer, an Employment Permit from the Department of Enterprise, Trade and Employment. No short engagement worked without either is modelled.

sources.title: Immigration Service Delivery (Department of Justice), Atypical Working Scheme
sources.said: In most cases where a non-EEA national wishes to work in Ireland, he or she must apply to the Department of Enterprise, Trade and Employment (DETE) for an Employment Permit. ... in order to facilitate specialised, highly-skilled employment of a short term nature (generally less than 90 days) that is not supported by current Employment Permit legislation. ... Permission under the Scheme is granted for a maximum period of 90 days ... The above measures apply only to the “general” category of applications for permission under the Scheme (including the entertainment industry, biotech, pharmaceutical, and technology sectors)

sources.title: GOV.UK, Common Travel Area guidance
sources.said: Under the CTA , British and Irish citizens can move freely and reside in either jurisdiction and enjoy associated rights and privileges, including the right to work, study and vote in certain elections
